newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan guru impassive as witness recalls gas attack.
newsitem.headline: Japan guru impassive as witness recalls gas attack.

text.p: Japanese doomsday cult leader Shoko Asahara on Thursday sat impassively through his first courtroom encounter with witnesses to last year's poison gas attack on the Tokyo subway.

Asahara, accused of ordering disciples of his Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect) to release the deadly nerve gas sarin on rush-hour subway trains in March 1995, showed no emotion as a subway worker described the attack, which killed 11 people and made 5,500 ill.
As in his six previous appearances in court, Asahara, 41, refused to enter a plea on any of the 17 murder, attempted murder and weapons and drug production charges he faces.

Subway employee Toshiaki Toyoda told Tokyo District Court of the frantic morning when two of his co-workers were gassed to death at central Tokyo's Kasumigaseki subway station, the main target of the attack.
"I smelled a foul odour of a kind I had never experienced in my life," he told the court.
Toyoda told how he and co-workers Kazumasa Takahashi and Tsuneo Hishinuma, who both later died, struggled to remove the strange substance from rush-hour subway cars.
"Mr Takahashi lay there with his eyes open but gave no response when I called him," said Toyoda, the first of five witnesses to appear in court.
Toyoda wrapped the sarin-filled plastic bags in newspapers and then passed out. He said he later spent six weeks in hospital in serious condition.
Asahara's trial resumed on Thursday after a two-month summer recess.
With the court sessions moving at a snail's pace, public interest has waned.
In contrast with the first trial date in April, when some 12,000 people queued for some 30 gallery seats, there were empty spectator seats in court on Thursday.
Interest is expected to pick up later this month, however, with a confrontation between Asahara, whose real name is Chizuo Matsumoto, and his disciples.

The sect's doctor, Ikuo Hayashi, and Asahara's lieutenant Yoshihiro Inoue, both accused of taking part in the subway attack, will testify on the alleged role Asahara played in the gassing in court hearings set for September 19 and 20.

In court appearances in separate trials so far, most followers have blamed Asahara for ordering gassings, weapons production and murders which kept Japan in a state of near panic for months last year.

One factor delaying court proceedings, aside from the scale and complexity of the crimes, is the determination of Asahara's court-appointed defence lawyers to scrutinise every legal detail before having him enter pleas.
The defence grilled the police witnesses for minor discrepancies in their official reports of the crime scene, which in the end drew yawns from the audience.

After the five witnesses finished their testimony, the judge and prosecutors urged Asahara's lawyers to explain why the guru continued to maintain his silence, criticising the defence for prolonging the preceedings by failing to clarify the points of argument in the trial.
The lawyers said the law does not require defendants to enter a plea and that the prosecutors' reluctance to disclose all evidence is one reason why Asahara had not done so.
"It's the prosecution's negligence," one lawyer said.
